headline: Hudson Canyon sets up for early-season yellowfin as 70-degree water creeps north
subhead: With live buoy and SST feeds running thin, the 100-fathom edge and the Dip remain the highest-probability structure on the first push of warm water.
body_markdown:
The oceanographic picture for the canyon this week is being read with a thinner-than-usual stack of data. The Dr. Fish analyst flagged real gaps — no current tide station feed, the SST package hasn't refreshed since June 3, and there's been no fresh offshore video intelligence since the 4th. That matters, because at this point in the season the chlorophyll break and the warm tongue moving up the shelf can shift ten miles in 48 hours, and we're flying without the most recent thermal imagery. The most recent published SST packages — May 31 through June 3 — showed the 68 to 70 degree water pressing against the 100-fathom line on the western wall of the Hudson, with cleaner blue pushing into the notch between the Claw and the Dip. Without a June 4 or June 5 frame to confirm, the working assumption is that warm water has continued its northwest drift and the temperature break sits somewhere along the upper canyon edge in 70 to 90 fathoms.

For a Hudson beat in early June, that structure read means one thing: the first real yellowfin shot of the season is setting up on the west wall, and the fish that show will be running with the warm push. This is not yet the August stack on the tip — it's the leading edge, scattered schools of 40 to 70 pound yellowfin tracking the thermocline as it tightens. The Dip and the upper canyon notches are the spots that fire first because the bathymetry forces upwelling on the inside of the warm flow, pinning sand eels and small squid against the shelf break. Run the troll at first light along the 100-fathom contour from the Claw down to the Dip, ballyhoo and small spreader bars in the pattern, and pay attention to surface temperature gradients of even half a degree across a quarter mile — that's the line you want to work.

Bluefin remain the other half of the early-June equation. The medium and large class fish that have been chewing inside of the canyon on the 30-fathom lumps don't read SST charts the same way the yellowfin do — they're keying on sand eel biomass and water clarity, and the inshore-to-offshore thermal structure between the 30-fathom line and the 100-fathom line is still steep enough to hold them on the inside. Jigging and popping on marks is producing better than trolling for that class right now, and the bite has been more of a midday slack-water event than a dawn pattern. If a crew is running out and the canyon edge looks soft, the lumps inside of Texas Tower are the consolation prize that's been paying.

Swordfish are the quiet story. Daytime deep-dropping along the canyon walls in 1,500 to 1,800 feet has been a steady program for boats willing to commit the day to it, and the lack of strong surface current right now — based on the last verified analyst window — makes for workable rigs without 12 pounds of lead. The fish are laying on the bottom of the canyon temperature column where it stabilizes in the high 40s, and a properly presented squid bait at depth will get bit. It's not a numbers game; it's a one-good-bite game, but that one bite is often a qualifier.

Looking ahead three to five days, the variable to watch is wind. A sustained southwest flow will push the warm tongue harder against the shelf and accelerate the yellowfin migration up the edge — that's the scenario that turns the Dip on. A northeast blow does the opposite, scatters the break, and pushes the cleaner water back offshore. The new moon falls into this window as well, and historically the dark-of-the-moon chunk bite on the canyon tip starts producing the first real overnight yellowfin reports of the season right around this calendar slot. I'd be planning a 36-hour trip for late this week with a chunk set on the troll-up.

The Hudson is doing exactly what the Hudson does in the first week of June — leaking warm water onto the shelf, staging bait against the edge, and rewarding the boats that commit to fishing the structure rather than chasing rumors. Until the SST pipeline catches up and the buoy feeds come back clean, run the contour, read the surface, and trust the canyon.
